records.title: Product Engineering intern
records.summary: Built and integrated Python backend services and REST APIs for a B2B product, and prototyped new product capabilities from requirements through to working software.
records.body:
## What the work actually involved

I joined Majara as a product engineering intern, working hybrid out of
Riyadh. The team is small, so the role spans further than a typical
internship: building backend services in Python, wiring up REST APIs
for the frontend and integrations to consume, and prototyping product
capabilities that started as a requirements conversation rather than
a finished spec.

A lot of the work sat at the intersection of "figure out what's
actually being asked for" and "make it work in production" — reading
a stakeholder's description of a workflow, translating it into a data
model and an API surface, then iterating once real usage showed the
gaps in the first pass. LangChain came in for the pieces that needed
to reason over unstructured input rather than follow a fixed branch of
logic.

The B2B product context mattered: customers are companies, not
individuals, so multi-tenancy, permissions, and predictable behavior
under someone else's business process were constant constraints, not
edge cases to handle later.

records.title: Business Development Intern
records.summary: Ran client meetings, prepared sales pitches, presented proposals, and managed ongoing client relationships. It taught me to read what a client actually needs and present a practical solution — the other half of the problem-solving process from the engineering side.
records.body:
## What the work actually involved

Before Majara, I spent a few months in business development at SEET
(صيت), a marketing solutions agency in Riyadh. The role was almost the
inverse of engineering work: instead of starting from a technical
requirement, I started from a client conversation and had to figure
out what solution actually fit, then make the case for it.

Day to day that meant running client meetings, putting together sales
pitches and proposal decks, presenting them, and staying in the loop
on the relationship afterward rather than treating a signed deal as
the end of the interaction. Clients rarely describe their problem in a
form that maps directly onto a service line, so a lot of the value was
in translation — turning a vague complaint or goal into a concrete,
sellable scope.

I think about this experience often on the engineering side now: a
badly scoped technical requirement and a badly scoped sales pitch fail
for the same reason, and the fix is the same skill — sit with the
client or stakeholder until you understand what they actually need,
not just what they first said.

records.title: Corporate hotel booking backend
records.summary: A FastAPI service that turns bulk employee trip requests into booked hotels — Amadeus search, bulk booking through Celery workers, and confirmation emails. I built the core flows solo: multi-tenant, idempotent, with retry and backoff around a rate-limited external API. Shelved before launch when industry regulations changed.
records.body:
## What the work actually involved

This was a FastAPI backend for a corporate travel workflow: a company
submits a bulk trip request for a group of employees, and the system
has to turn that into actual booked hotel rooms. I built the core
flows solo.

The shape of the problem was mostly about talking to an external,
rate-limited API (Amadeus) reliably at scale. Search and booking calls
ran through Celery workers rather than inline in the request/response
cycle, both to keep the API responsive and to get retry and
exponential backoff around calls that would otherwise fail under
normal Amadeus rate limits. Idempotency was a hard requirement —
retrying a failed booking call must never double-book a room or double-
charge a client, so every booking operation carried an idempotency key
and the write path was built to be safely repeatable.

The service was multi-tenant from the start: each corporate client's
requests, bookings, and traveler data needed to stay isolated from
every other client sharing the same deployment. Postgres (via
SQLAlchemy) held the booking and tenant state, Redis backed the Celery
queue, and confirmation emails went out once a booking cleared.

The project was shelved before launch when industry regulations
changed in a way that affected the booking model it was built around —
not a technical failure, but the kind of external shift that can kill
a project regardless of how solid the implementation is.

records.title: About
records.summary: Backend-leaning software engineer based in Riyadh, currently interning at Majara and building this site's own AI chat feature as a hands-on exercise in RAG and agent orchestration.
records.body:
## Who I am

I'm a software engineer based in Riyadh, currently interning at Majara
as a product engineering intern, where I work on Python backend
services, REST APIs, and new product prototypes for a B2B platform.
Before that I spent a few months in business development at SEET
(صيت), a Riyadh marketing agency, which is where I picked up the habit
of treating "what does the other side actually need" as the first
question in any project, technical or not.

Most of my hands-on engineering experience so far centers on backend
work: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, REST API design, and the
infrastructure around that (Postgres, Redis, Celery, Docker, pytest).
I'm comfortable moving from a requirements conversation to a working
system, and I care about the parts of backend work that don't show up
in a demo — idempotency, retries, multi-tenancy, and what happens when
an external dependency misbehaves.

This portfolio site's chat feature is a deliberate exception to how I
otherwise approach projects: where I usually default to the simplest
tool that solves the problem, the chat feature is a dedicated learning
exercise, so I chose heavier architecture on purpose — retrieval over
this markdown corpus, agent orchestration with LangGraph, and
self-hosting the backend on my own infrastructure — specifically to
get hands-on practice with those pieces rather than to keep the site
itself minimal.

records.title: Are you available for work?
records.summary: Currently interning at Majara; open to hearing about new opportunities, best reached through the contact details on this site.
records.body:
## Availability

I'm currently interning at Majara in a product engineering role. That
doesn't mean I'm off the market — I'm happy to hear about new
opportunities, and the best way to reach me is through the contact
details on this site.

If you're asking because you're evaluating me for a role: my strongest
fit is backend-leaning engineering work — API design, service
integrations, and systems that need to hold up under real usage, not
just a demo. I'm still early in my career, so I'm looking for roles
that give me room to keep growing rather than assuming I already have
every answer.
